setting.name: Control Power Watchdog Timeout Cluster
setting.casual_explanation: This cluster appears to define multiple watchdog timeout defaults inside the power manager. The values are documented in repo notes, but they are not present in the observed clean registry baseline.
setting.why_people_change_it: Kernel and power researchers may inspect these values when investigating watchdog timeout behavior around driver monitor, DWM sync flush, Po callouts, power-on GDI, and request queue paths.
setting.tradeoffs_overview: The cluster has explicit doc defaults, clean baseline evidence, a broad no-hit current-build string pass, and now one exact helper-triggered ETW query for `PowerWatchdogPoCalloutTimeoutMsec`. It still lacks a broader current-build structural pivot or boot-consumer trace, so it should stay in the research queue as a family hold rather than a tweak candidate.
setting.professional_notes: The repo docs list five `Control\\Power` watchdog defaults under `InitializePowerWatchdogTimeoutDefaults`: `PowerWatchdogDrvSetMonitorTimeoutMsec = 10000`, `PowerWatchdogDwmSyncFlushTimeoutMsec = 30000`, `PowerWatchdogPoCalloutTimeoutMsec = 10000`, `PowerWatchdogPowerOnGdiTimeoutMsec = 30000`, and `PowerWatchdogRequestQueueTimeoutMsec = 30000`. The docs-first power routing pass already grouped them as new `Control\\Power` candidates. The observed clean baseline existence pass later confirmed that the parent `Control\\Power` path exists while all five registry values are absent. The broad current-build string batch then returned clean `no-hit` results for all five values, which is stronger than a vague unknown but still weaker than a real current-build symbol or caller clue. A later targeted host-side `ntoskrnl.exe` check also found no exact `PowerWatchdogTimeout` string; retained watchdog Ghidra artifacts are adjacent DPC/profile or Win32 callout evidence, not a direct reader/seeding path for this five-value `Control\\Power` cluster. Existing enrichment output already converges on the same next runtime family for all five values: `power-request-simulation`, low runtime priority, `windbg` queue. The cluster therefore deserves a schema-backed draft, but it is intentionally held until a targeted binary probe or new runtime trace provides a stronger current-build path-aware lead. A later 2026-04-23 skip-tracerpt ETW stackwalk rerun then used the repaired host runner to backfill a guest-side tracerpt XML sidecar and produced one exact helper-triggered `RegQueryValue` event for `PowerWatchdogPoCalloutTimeoutMsec`, with a `reg.exe` -> `KernelBase.dll` / `ntdll.dll` -> `ntoskrnl.exe` stack and status `0xC0000034`. That closes parser visibility for one cluster member but still does not provide a named current-build seeding or consumer path for the broader family.

evidence.title: KVM ETW stackwalk captures exact PowerWatchdogPoCalloutTimeoutMsec RegQueryValue
evidence.summary: After fixing the host ETW stackwalk ingest path to backfill guest-generated tracerpt XML when host-side tracerpt is unavailable, a QGA-launched 45-second capture produced a physical ETL, XML sidecar, and normalized bundle for `PowerWatchdogPoCalloutTimeoutMsec`. The bundle contains one exact `RegQueryValue` event for `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Power` / `PowerWatchdogPoCalloutTimeoutMsec`, with caller stack frames through `reg.exe`, `KernelBase.dll`, `ntdll.dll`, and `ntoskrnl.exe`; the returned status `0xC0000034` shows the value is absent on the clean baseline. This upgrades parser/runtime visibility for one cluster member while leaving the broader family unresolved.

decision.why: The family is strong enough for a schema-backed draft because it has explicit repo-doc defaults, a clean observed-baseline state, a broad current-build no-hit string pass, enrichment guidance, and now an exact helper-triggered ETW stackwalk `RegQueryValue` event for `PowerWatchdogPoCalloutTimeoutMsec`. It is still not ready for validation or tweak exposure because the current build lacks a broader named symbol/string/caller pivot for the five-value family, the exact query is helper-triggered rather than boot-consumer proof, and Microsoft does not publish a primary current-build contract for these internal defaults.
